title: Discovery in a civil action
intro: This guide explains what the Rules of Civil Procedure say about discovery in a Superior Court of Justice action: the discovery plan, proportionality, sharing documents, and examinations for discovery, whether oral or by written questions.

sections.heading: The discovery plan
paragraphs: Where a party intends to obtain evidence under the discovery rules, including Rule 30 (Discovery of Documents), Rule 31 (Examination for Discovery) and Rule 35 (Examination for Discovery by Written Questions), “the parties to the action shall agree to a discovery plan”. The plan is agreed before the earlier of “60 days after the close of pleadings or such longer period as the parties may agree to” and attempting to obtain the evidence. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.03 (1), (2))

“The discovery plan shall be in writing”. It includes the intended scope of documentary discovery, dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents, information on the timing, costs and manner of producing documents, and “the names of persons intended to be produced for oral examination for discovery under Rule 31 and information respecting the timing and length of the examinations”. The parties “shall ensure that the discovery plan is updated”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.03 (3), 29.1.04)

On a discovery motion, “the court may refuse to grant any relief or to award any costs if the parties have failed to agree to or update a discovery plan”. If the parties fail to agree, the court may order examinations “in accordance with a discovery plan established by the court”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.05 (1), (2))

sections.heading: Proportionality
paragraphs: When deciding whether a party or other person must answer a question or produce a document, the court shall consider whether the time required “would be unreasonable”, whether the expense “would be unjustified”, whether it “would cause him or her undue prejudice”, whether it “would unduly interfere with the orderly progress of the action”, and whether the information or document “is readily available to the party requesting it from another source.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.2.03 (1))

For documents, the court also considers “whether such an order would result in an excessive volume of documents required to be produced by the party or other person.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.2.03 (2))

sections.heading: Documentary discovery and the affidavit of documents
paragraphs: For these rules, “document” includes “a sound recording, videotape, film, photograph, chart, graph, map, plan, survey, book of account, and data and information in electronic form”. “Every document relevant to any matter in issue in an action that is or has been in the possession, control or power of a party to the action shall be disclosed”, “whether or not privilege is claimed in respect of the document.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.01 (1) (a), 30.02 (1))

A party “shall serve on every other party an affidavit of documents (Form 30A or 30B)”. It lists, in separate schedules, relevant documents the party does not object to producing, documents for which the party claims privilege “and the grounds for the claim”, and documents no longer in the party's possession, control or power, with a statement of when and how that happened and their present location. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.03 (1), (2))

A party who serves a request to inspect documents (Form 30C) “is entitled to inspect any document that is not privileged and that is referred to in the other party's affidavit of documents”. The party served names a date “within five days after the service of the request”. “An affidavit of documents shall not be filed unless it is relevant to an issue on a pending motion or at trial.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.03 (5), 30.04 (1), (3))

If a party later obtains a relevant non-privileged document, or finds the affidavit inaccurate or incomplete, “the party shall forthwith serve a supplementary affidavit”. Disclosing or producing a document “shall not be taken as an admission of its relevance or admissibility.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.05, 30.07)

sections.heading: Privilege and failing to disclose
paragraphs: Relevant documents must be produced for inspection if requested, “unless privilege is claimed in respect of the document.” “Where privilege is claimed for a document, the court may inspect the document to determine the validity of the claim.” Rule 30 does not explain what privilege is, and this site does not yet have a source that does. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.02 (2), 30.04 (6))

A party that claims privilege for a document and does not abandon the claim, by giving notice in writing and providing a copy of the document or producing it for inspection, “at least 90 days before the commencement of the trial”, “may not use the document at the trial, except to impeach the testimony of a witness or with leave of the trial judge.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.09)

If a party fails to disclose a document in an affidavit of documents or supplementary affidavit, or fails to produce it as required by the rules, a court order or an undertaking, then if the document is favourable to the party's case, “the party may not use the document at the trial, except with leave of the trial judge”. If it is not favourable, “the court may make such order as is just.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.08 (1))

If a party fails to serve an affidavit of documents, fails to produce a document for inspection as the rules require, or fails to comply with an order under rules 30.02 to 30.11, the court may, among other things, “dismiss the action, if the party is a plaintiff, or strike out the statement of defence, if the party is a defendant”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.08 (2))

On a motion by a party, the court may order a non-party to produce a non-privileged document for inspection where it is satisfied that “the document is relevant to a material issue in the action” and “it would be unfair to require the moving party to proceed to trial without having discovery of the document.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.10 (1))

sections.heading: Examination for discovery: who, when and how long
paragraphs: An examination for discovery “may take the form of an oral examination or, at the option of the examining party, an examination by written questions and answers”, but not both without leave. Where more than one party is entitled to examine a person, the examination is oral “unless all the parties entitled to examine the person agree otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.02 (1), (2))
A party “may examine for discovery any other party adverse in interest, once”, and more than once only with leave of the court. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.03 (1))

A party may examine more than one person only as subrules 31.03 (2) to (8) permit. For example, where a corporation may be examined, the examining party may examine any officer, director or employee on its behalf, but more than one “only with the consent of the parties or the leave of the court.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.03 (1), (2))

A party who seeks to examine a plaintiff may serve a notice of examination or written questions “only after delivering a statement of defence and, unless the parties agree otherwise, serving an affidavit of documents.” A defendant may be examined after delivering a defence (with the examining party's affidavit of documents served, unless agreed otherwise) or after being noted in default. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.04 (1), (2))

“No party shall, in conducting oral examinations for discovery, exceed a total of seven hours of examination, regardless of the number of parties or other persons to be examined, except with the consent of the parties or with leave of the court.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.05.1 (1))

In an action under the simplified procedure (Rule 76), “no party shall, in conducting oral examinations for discovery in relation to an action proceeding under this Rule, exceed a total of three hours of examination, regardless of the number of parties or other persons to be examined.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.04 (2))

sections.heading: Examination for discovery: scope and answers
paragraphs: A person examined “shall answer, to the best of his or her knowledge, information and belief, any proper question relevant to any matter in issue in the action”. A question may not be objected to on the ground that “the information sought is evidence”. A party may also obtain “the names and addresses of persons who might reasonably be expected to have knowledge of transactions or occurrences in issue in the action, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.06 (1), (2))

A party, or a person examined on behalf of or in place of a party, fails to answer if they refuse, or if a question taken under advisement or an undertaking is not answered “within 60 days after the response.” The party then “may not introduce at the trial the information that was not provided, except with leave of the trial judge.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.07 (1), (2))

If a party later finds an answer “was incorrect or incomplete when made” or “is no longer correct and complete”, “the party shall forthwith provide the information in writing to every other party.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.09 (1))

The court may grant leave to examine for discovery a person “who there is reason to believe has information relevant to a material issue in the action”, other than an expert engaged by or for a party in preparation for contemplated or pending litigation. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.10 (1))

Leave is granted only if the court is satisfied that the moving party could not obtain the information from persons it is entitled to examine or from that person, that it would be unfair to proceed to trial without examining the person, and that the examination will not unduly delay the trial, entail unreasonable expense for other parties or be unfair to the person. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.10 (2))

sections.heading: How oral examinations are conducted
paragraphs: Where a party acts in person, a notice of examination (Form 34A) is served on the party “personally or by an alternative to personal service.” A person to be examined who resides in Ontario “shall be given not less than two days notice of the time and place of the examination, unless the court orders otherwise.” Every other party is also given not less than two days notice. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.04 (1), 34.05 (1), (2))

The person examined “shall take an oath or make an affirmation”. They produce the non-privileged documents rule 30.04 (4) requires, and those the notice of examination requires. Where a question is objected to, “the objector shall state briefly the reason for the objection, and the question and the brief statement shall be recorded.” A ruling may be obtained on motion. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.08 (1), 34.10 (2), 34.12 (1), (3))

An examination may be adjourned to seek directions where, for example, it “is being conducted in bad faith, or in an unreasonable manner so as to annoy, embarrass or oppress the person being examined”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.14 (1))

If a person fails to attend, or refuses to answer a proper question or produce a required document, the court may, among other things, order the person to reattend and answer where an objection is held to be improper, and, where the person is a party or is examined on a party's behalf, “dismiss the party's proceeding or strike out the party's defence”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.15 (1))

“Every examination shall be recorded in its entirety in question and answer form in a manner that permits the preparation of a typed transcript”, unless ordered or agreed otherwise. On request, a typed transcript is to be completed “within four weeks after receipt of the request.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.16, 34.17 (1))

sections.heading: Examination by written questions
paragraphs: A written examination is conducted “by serving a list of the questions to be answered (Form 35A) on the person to be examined and every other party.” The questions are answered by affidavit (Form 35B), served on the examining party “within fifteen days after service of the list of questions.” An objection is made in the affidavit “with a brief statement of the reason for the objection.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 35.01, 35.02 (1), 35.03)

If the examining party is not satisfied with an answer, it may, “within ten days after receiving the answer, serve a further list of written questions which shall be answered within fifteen days after service.” If answers are “evasive, unresponsive or otherwise unsatisfactory”, the court may order an oral examination. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 35.04 (1), (3))

“Examination for discovery by written questions and answers under Rule 35” is “not permitted in an action under this Rule”, meaning an action under the simplified procedure. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.04 (1))
